node.label: Keith Thomas
node.date_label: “History and Anthropology” (1963) · Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) · Man and the Natural World (1983)
node.description: A historian of early modern English beliefs, social relations and attitudes. Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) asks why beliefs in magic, astrology and witchcraft made sense in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century England and why they declined; the inquiry began, he recalls, from a puzzle about astrology and led him to anthropology. His 1963 essay ‘History and Anthropology’ grew from a review of Evans-Pritchard that Lawrence Stone encouraged him to expand. Thomas names Christopher Hill and R. H. Tawney as formative influences, and was drawn to Lucien Febvre’s inquiry into people’s assumptions rather than to quantitative Annales history. He later called his work a descriptive ethnography of early modern England and conceded that his explanation of magic’s decline was incomplete. Jan Machielsen and Michelle Pfeffer’s 2023 reassessment, building on Hildred Geertz’s criticism, questions the book’s categories of religion and magic. Man and the Natural World (1983) traced changing English attitudes to nature.

proposed_edges.relationship: Uses anthropology to make historical belief intelligible while retaining an empirically particular form of inquiry.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Machielsen and Pfeffer, section II, paragraphs associated with notes 56–73. The named readers distinguish theoretical borrowing from ethnographic accumulation and retain Geertz’s objection; no direct reading of the original 1963 manifesto is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Investigates past belief in magic and religion; his categories and account of decline have since been contested.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Machielsen and Pfeffer (2023), opening and section III. Verified 2026-10-31.

proposed_edges.relationship: Provides Stone with an example of arranging historical stories around an argument.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Existing source’s bounded primary Stone reading, pp. 3–6 and 13–24 only, and the preserved Keith Thomas roster context. Not Thomas’s assent to all of Stone’s narrative-revival diagnosis.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas identifies Hill as his main undergraduate intellectual influence and recalls the high scholarly expectations of his teaching.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Part 1, 51:15:24, explicit retrospective testimony. Bounded training influence, not automatic adoption of Hill’s Marxism.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas identifies Tawney as a deep intellectual influence while distinguishing admiration from copying historical models.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Part 2, 43:02:10; part 1 school-reading recollection supplies additional context only. No claim of fresh Tawney reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas credits the Febvre strand of Annales with encouraging inquiry into historical values and mental assumptions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Part 2, 36:50:21, explicitly distinguishes that attraction from hard quantitative Annales. Not allegiance to all Annales methods.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas credits Stone with encouraging the expansion of his Evans-Pritchard review into the history-and-anthropology intervention.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Part 2, 16:43:03. Concrete publication encouragement and conceptual discussion, not the source of every anthropological idea.
